headline: AI coding assistants can expose your API keys; new tool 'concealer' encrypts them locally
summary: Your .env file secrets are vulnerable to AI coding assistants. A new open-source tool, 'concealer', offers local-only encryption, ensuring agents can use secrets without ever seeing them.
details: AI coding assistants, designed to read your repository for usefulness, can inadvertently expose sensitive API keys stored in plaintext .env files. This creates new leak paths that did not exist when .env was a secure compromise.

The open-source tool 'concealer' addresses this by acting as a local-only AI Secret Manager. It keeps your secrets encrypted and on your machine, allowing AI agents to utilize them without ever directly accessing the plaintext values.

Built on battle-tested tools like SOPS and age, concealer offers typed secrets, project/environment scoping, a web console, and a tamper-evident audit log. Crucially, it includes an MCP (Model Context Protocol) server for secure agent interaction.

The MCP server enables agents to ask for secret names and request concealer to run commands with those named secrets. The plaintext value is injected only into the child process, never entering the agent's context, and outputs are redacted.

This system acts like a 'valet key': the agent can perform tasks requiring secrets but never holds the key itself. concealer also guards against bulk theft by limiting access to one secret per agent request, with a rate limit.

concealer is a single Python 3 script with no cloud, no account, and no telemetry. It's designed to be portable and focuses on local encryption, ensuring your sensitive data remains on your machine and out of AI context windows.

headline: Cut your AI bill by 45% with this trick nobody explains to small businesses
summary: Understanding 'cache economics' can slash your AI costs by up to 45% for the same service, a crucial detail often overlooked by small businesses comparing sticker prices.
details: Many businesses comparison-shop AI tools by their sticker price, but this often overlooks a critical factor: cache economics. This principle can cut your AI bill by nearly half without needing to switch tools or models.

When sending a prompt to an AI model, a significant portion of the tokens (e.g., 9,000 out of 10,000) often remain identical across multiple calls. Only a small part, like the specific question or data, changes each time.

The key to savings lies in how AI vendors charge for these repeated tokens. Some providers recognize and cache this repeated context, charging less for the cached portion because they don't reprocess it from scratch every time.

For example, when Anthropic released Claude Fable 5.1, its sticker price was the same as Fable 5. However, a quiet drop in the cache read price cut real-world costs by approximately 45% for heavy users with consistent context.

Small businesses often lack the procurement specialists that enterprises use to model total cost of ownership. This means they might pay full price for the same repeated 9,000 tokens on every call if their vendor doesn't optimize for cache economics.

Before committing to an AI tool or API, ask vendors if they cache repeated context, what they charge for cached reads, and what percentage of your typical prompt is cacheable. A blank stare is a red flag.

Controlling your context (system prompts, business documents) is crucial. This allows you to test new providers for caching efficiency before migrating, preventing vendor lock-in and ensuring you're not paying full price unnecessarily.
